U0600.d: Newer engines often use a digital oil pressure sensor that sends its value over a SENT line (SAE J2716) instead of an analog voltage. SENT is a one-way link with a 5 V supply, a signal wire and ground; each frame carries a CRC and a status nibble.
s: Check engine light on
Oil pressure warning or no oil pressure reading
c: Open, shorted or chafed SENT signal, supply or ground wire
Oil or corrosion in the sensor connector

U0601.d: Particulate filter pressure sensor A measures the pressure drop across a diesel or gasoline particulate filter, the basis for soot load estimates and filter monitoring. Digital versions report over SENT.
s: Check engine light, on GM already in the first trip
Filter regeneration may run on a model only or be blocked
Reduced power on some diesels
c: SENT line, 5 V supply or ground interrupted or shorted
Sensor internal fault switching off its output (heat, moisture)

U0602.d: Pressure sensor B serves a second particulate filter or a second measuring point, for example on engines with one gasoline particulate filter per bank. The code means its digital SENT output has stopped delivering usable frames to the engine controller.
s: Check engine light on
Particulate filter monitor for the affected branch incomplete
c: Damaged SENT, supply or ground wire to sensor B
Loose or corroded connector at sensor B

U0603.d: Fuel pressure sensor A reports fuel or rail pressure, which the controller needs for injection quantity and pump control. When the sensor is digital, it transmits over a point-to-point SENT line instead of an analog voltage, and U0603 means its frames no longer arrive in usable form: wire open or shorted, signal stuck high or low, CRC errors or an internal sensor fault.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Hard start, stalling or no start
c: SENT signal, 5 V supply or ground wire faulty

U0604.d: Sensor B is the second fuel pressure measuring point, for example a low-pressure sensor in the feed line of a direct injection engine or a second rail on V engines; which pressure it reads depends on the maker. U0604 flags that this digital sensor has stopped sending valid SENT frames to the engine controller.
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation or reduced power under load
c: Damaged signal, supply or ground wire to sensor B
Sensor A and B connectors swapped or loose

U0605.d: The air conditioning controller needs refrigerant pressure or temperature to run the compressor and protect the circuit. Where this information comes over a serial link such as LIN, a single master polls the slave and expects an answer in a fixed schedule; U0605 means refrigerant sensor A no longer answers properly.
s: A/C does not cool
Compressor switched off by the controller
c: Open or shorted LIN, supply or ground wire to the sensor
Electric compressor shorted internally, high-voltage A/C fuse open (Mazda PHEV)

U0606.d: Many electronic throttle bodies now report the blade angle as digital SENT frames (SAE J2716) instead of two analog voltages. U0606 means the engine controller no longer receives valid frames from position sensor A.
s: Check engine light, on Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode with limited throttle response
Rough or unstable idle
c: SENT signal, 5 V supply or ground wire to the throttle body open, shorted or chafed
Loose, corroded or water-soaked throttle body connector
Sensor electronics in the throttle body failed (replacement usually as a complete throttle body)
Engine controller SENT input or software fault

U0607.d: Position sensor B is the redundant second track of a throttle or pedal unit. On SENT throttle bodies both tracks often share one sensor chip and even one frame (the dual throttle format A.1 of J2716), so a broken line usually drops A and B together.
s: Check engine light, on GM in the first trip
Limited power because the redundancy check is lost
c: Second sensor channel inside the throttle or pedal unit failed
Damaged SENT line, supply or ground (often sets U0606 as well)
Spread or corroded terminal at the sensor connector
Engine controller software decoding the second channel wrongly

U0608.d: Sensor C usually belongs to a second throttle body, as on engines with one throttle per bank or two throttles in parallel. Ford's 2020 to 2024 gasoline summaries spell this out: on dual-throttle applications the SENT sensor of throttle body B reports as sensor C, and U0608 sets with MIL and wrench lamp when wiring or the SENT device has been faulty for more than 4 s.
s: Check engine light and, on Ford, wrench lamp
Reduced power, uneven running between banks
c: Wiring fault on the SENT harness branch to the second throttle body
Position sensor electronics of the second throttle body failed
Corroded or loose connector at throttle body B

U0609.d: A digital manifold pressure sensor sends pressure, often with an intake temperature value, as SENT frames; chips built for this, such as Infineon's KP276, add a status nibble with error flags and a CRC to every frame. U0609 is stored when those frames stop arriving or cannot be used.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or limited boost
Rough running or harder starting at altitude
c: SENT line stuck low, open or chafed, or supply/ground missing
Sensor reports an internal fault (moisture, oil or soot ingress)

U060A.d: MAP sensor B is a second manifold pressure sensor, found for example on V engines with a separate intake plenum per bank or on engines measuring before and after the throttle. U060A applies when this sensor is digitally connected and the controller stops receiving usable SENT frames from it, whether because of a dead line, a broken frame or the sensor's own error code; Melexis' MLX90818, made for manifold and turbo p
s: Check engine light
Reduced power on the affected bank or intake path
c: Open, shorted or chafed wire to MAP sensor B
MAP sensor B electronics failed or reporting an internal error
Corroded or loose connector at sensor B

U060B.d: Boost sensor A measures charge air pressure after the compressor and is often a SENT pressure sensor with built-in temperature measurement. U060B means the engine controller no longer hears from it.
s: Check engine light
Noticeably less power, boost held low
Fault may come and go with engine vibration
c: Wires broken by vibration right behind the sensor connector
Loose terminal or oil in the connector

U060C.d: Boost sensor B is needed where charge pressure is measured twice: on twin-turbo V engines with one charge path per bank, on two-stage systems between the stages, or after the charge air cooler in addition to sensor A. When it is a digital SENT device, its frames carry pressure, often a temperature value, a status nibble and a CRC.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power with boost limited
c: Damaged wiring to boost sensor B, often near hot turbo plumbing
Loose or oil-soaked connector at sensor B

U060D.d: A third boost sensor C appears only on complex charging layouts, for instance sequential or two-stage turbo systems with pressure taps between and after the stages, or engines that add an electric compressor. U060D reports that the controller has lost the digital link to this sensor: no SENT frame inside the expected time, a frame failing its check, or a sensor that transmits only its reserved error value, a feature
s: Check engine light
Power loss when the affected stage would build boost
c: Open or shorted SENT, supply or ground wire to sensor C
Sensor C sending only its error value

U060E.d: A crankcase pressure sensor lets the engine controller check the positive crankcase ventilation for leaks or a disconnected hose, which CARB 1968.2 requires. Ford fits it in two versions.
s: Check engine light
Crankcase ventilation monitor does not complete
c: Damaged SENT, supply or ground wire to the crankcase pressure sensor
Oil or moisture in the sensor connector

U060F.d: Modern hot-film air flow meters often transmit digitally; Bosch lists SENT, frequency and LIN outputs, and many units also carry pressure, temperature or humidity. U060F means sensor A's messages are missing.
s: Check engine light, often together with an air flow circuit code
Engine runs on a modelled air mass, with reduced response
Rough idle or hesitation
c: Water, corrosion or loose terminals in the air flow sensor connector
LIN or SENT line, battery feed or ground to the sensor interrupted
Sporadic communication error without hardware fault (cleared and rechecked)

U0610.d: Air flow sensor B is the second meter on engines that measure each intake path separately, typically one per bank on V engines with two air boxes. In GM's documents 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07, written for an engine with two throttle bodies, U060F stands for bank 1 and U0610 for bank 2: the code sets when the digital sensor itself reports a time overflow or a maximum-period violation for 1.5 s with battery voltage above 9
s: Check engine light after the second trip on GM
Uneven running or slightly reduced power
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to air flow sensor B damaged
Air flow sensor B electronics failed or contaminated
Moisture or loose terminal at sensor B connector

U0611.d: Intake air temperature is often no longer a separate NTC wire to the controller but a value inside a digital frame: combined air flow meters send it over LIN or SENT, and pressure chips such as Infineon's KP276 digitize an attached NTC and pass it on in the same SENT message. U0611 concerns sensor 1 of bank 1, typically the upstream sensor in the air filter or air flow path.
s: Check engine light, on GM after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in driving
c: Wiring fault to the combined sensor that carries the temperature value
Electronics of the combined air flow or pressure sensor failed
Corroded or loose connector in the intake path

U0612.d: Bank 2 needs its own intake temperature sensor only where the engine has two separate air paths, as on V engines with one air box and throttle per bank. U0612 is the lost-communication code for that sensor 1 of bank 2.
s: Check engine light
Little effect on driving; with Ford's air flow sensor B reduced response possible
c: Wiring fault on the bank 2 intake sensor branch
Bank 2 temperature sensor or its host sensor failed (on Ford the air flow sensor B)
Corroded connector on the bank 2 intake

U0613.d: Intake air temperature sensor 2 sits further downstream than sensor 1, for example after the charge air cooler or in the manifold, where it is frequently combined with a pressure sensor (a TMAP unit). Digital versions send the temperature together with pressure; Melexis' MLX90818 can carry a medium temperature in its SENT frame and replaces the value with a reserved error code when measurement fails.
s: Check engine light, on GM after two trips
Possible spark retard or boost reduction as a precaution
c: Damaged wiring to the combined temperature/pressure sensor
Temperature element or electronics of the combined sensor failed
Oil from the charge air path in the connector

U0614.d: This is the bank 2 counterpart of U0613: the downstream intake temperature sensor of the second bank, usually after that bank's charge air cooler or in its manifold half, delivers its value digitally and the controller has stopped receiving it. Typical carriers are TMAP-style sensors whose SENT frames hold pressure and temperature, protected by a CRC and status bits, as described for Infineon's KP276.
s: Check engine light
Little effect on driving, occasionally less boost
c: Wiring fault to the bank 2 combined temperature/pressure sensor
Corroded or oily connector at the bank 2 sensor

U0615.d: Engines with split cooling circuits often route coolant through an electrically driven valve that reports its position and status digitally. U0615 is stored when the engine controller gets no answer from bypass valve A.
s: Check engine light
Little or no cabin heat
Engine warms up slower or coolant temperature behaves unusually
c: Moisture or corrosion in the valve connector (Ram bulletin 08-171-26)
LIN, supply or ground wire to the valve open, shorted or chafed
Valve actuator electronics failed (valve no longer answers)
LIN master in the engine controller faulty

U0616.d: Valve B is a second electronically controlled coolant valve, for example one that splits flow between the block and the head or toward a heater or oil cooler; which valve carries the letter B depends on the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents U0616 publicly.
s: Warning lamp, often without a noticeable change in driving
Unusual warm-up behaviour or coolant temperature swings
c: Damaged signal, supply or ground wire in the branch to valve B
Loose, corroded or wet connector at valve B
Controller software or configuration does not match the fitted valve

U0617.d: Unlike its LIN-based neighbours, GM uses U0617 for a coolant bypass valve whose position sensor transmits SENT frames (SAE J2716) to the engine controller. The tables 25OBDG03B and 25OBDG04B count a failure when the input hardware flags a message fault, when pulses arrive but the newest frame is older than 6.25 ms, or when the SENT pin voltage stays above or below a controller limit while frames go stale.
s: Check engine light (on GM after two trips, on 2019 calibrations after one)
Slow warm-up or reduced heater output
Possibly further coolant valve codes stored at the same time
c: SENT signal, 5 V supply or ground wire of the valve position sensor open or shorted
Corroded or loose connector at the valve
Position sensor inside the valve failed (usually replaced with the valve)
SENT input of the engine controller faulty

U0618.d: Bypass valve D is a fourth smart coolant valve and appears only on engines with several separately controlled coolant paths. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG03B is the one public document found that uses U0618: the engine controller polls the valve over LIN and expects its response frame (BRV_Rsp).
s: Check engine light after two trips
Unusual coolant temperature or warm-up behaviour
c: LIN wire, supply or ground to valve D interrupted or chafed
Poor contact at the valve connector
Fault on the shared LIN bus or in the LIN master (several LIN codes)

U0619.d: Reductant level sensor A reports how much diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) is left in the SCR tank. Newer tank units are smart sensors: a sensing element plus electronics that transmit level, temperature and often concentration as digital frames over CAN, SENT or LIN.
s: Check engine light or SCR warning
DEF gauge blank or frozen at a fixed value
No warning before the DEF tank runs empty
c: Corroded, water-soaked or loose connector at the DEF tank sensor
Data line, supply or ground of the tank sensor chafed or broken along the frame
Electronics of the tank level sensor failed (often replaced as a tank sender unit)
Controller software or configuration not matching the installed sensor

U061A.d: Some SCR tanks carry more than one level measurement, for example a second sensing element, a second tank chamber or a separate sender; which point counts as B is the manufacturer's choice, and no public document assigns it. U061A is stored when the controller stops receiving usable digital frames from level sensor B while sensor A may still report normally.
s: Check engine light or DEF system warning
DEF level shown wrongly or not at all
c: Open or chafed wire in the branch that feeds only level sensor B
Water or corrosion in the connector of sensor B

U061B.d: Level sensor C is a third level input of a reductant system and exists only on layouts with more than one tank or measuring point. No manufacturer publicly documents U061B or explains which part carries the letter C.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp
Implausible DEF quantity on the display
c: Damaged pins, corrosion or water in the connector of sensor C
Harness to the additional tank or measuring point damaged
Internal failure of level sensor C

U061C.d: Reductant temperature sensor A tells the controller how warm the diesel exhaust fluid is. That value decides when tank and line heaters must run, when dosing may begin after a cold start, and the concentration reading relies on it, since it is calculated from how fast sound travels through the fluid.
s: Check engine light
DEF heater or SCR dosing starts late or not at all in cold weather
DEF quality reading unavailable
c: Connector of the combined DEF tank sensor corroded or loose
Damaged data, supply or ground wire to the sensor
Sensor electronics failed, sometimes after freeze damage

U061D.d: Temperature sensor B is a second temperature input of the reductant system. Where it sits depends on the maker: at another spot in the tank unit, in the pump or supply module, or along the dosing line.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp
Line or pump heating may not work properly in frost
c: Wiring to the second temperature point (pump module or dosing line) damaged
Connector of temperature sensor B corroded or not latched
Temperature sensor B or the module housing it failed

U061E.d: A battery isolation or voltage stabilization module separates a second 12 V battery or protected loads from the starter circuit, so that cranking during an automatic restart does not drag the voltage of the rest of the vehicle down. A GM patent (US 9,803,608) describes such an isolator built from MOSFET switches.
s: Powertrain malfunction (wrench) lamp on Ford trucks
Additional battery or isolator code such as P2C44
c: Poor ground connection of the isolator circuit (Ford ground GD132)
Weak or deeply discharged auxiliary battery
Communication wire or connector to the module damaged

U061F.d: Many current exhaust temperature sensors are active: a thermocouple probe, often type N, feeds a small electronics module that turns the reading into SENT or CAN messages, as in the Sensience 22J sensor. U061F means valid messages from the bank 1, position 1 sensor (normally the most upstream one) have stopped.
s: Check engine or emission warning lamp
Further codes for the controller input or the second bank
Particulate filter regeneration may be postponed
c: Sensor harness rubbing through on a bracket or subframe edge (Bentley V8)
Connector or module of the sensor damaged by exhaust heat
Internal fault of the active sensor that shuts its SENT output off
Missing 5 V supply or ground from the controller

U0620.d: Sensor 2 on bank 1 is the next exhaust temperature measuring point downstream of sensor 1; on diesels it usually sits ahead of the particulate filter or the SCR catalyst, depending on how the maker numbers its sensors. U0620 is the lost-communication code for this point when it is a digital sensor: its frames have stopped, are too old, or its own diagnosis has switched the SENT output off.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp in the first trip on GM diesels
Diesel particulate filter or SCR warnings may follow
c: Signal, supply or ground wire of the sensor damaged near the exhaust
Moisture or corrosion in the underbody connector

U0621.d: U0621 mirrors U061F on bank 2: messages from the first exhaust temperature sensor of the second cylinder bank no longer reach the controller, so the code only appears on V engines or other layouts with two exhaust paths. Bentley documents it for the V8 in the Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur, model years 2020 to 2023 (bulletins 2065698/1 and 2065698/2): the emission warning lamp is lit and the fault memory shows U
s: Emission warning lamp on
Code logged as intermittent first, later static
c: Harness rubbed through on the subframe or a wheel-arch bracket
Electronics of the bank 2 sensor failed

U0622.d: U0622 covers the second exhaust temperature measuring point on bank 2 when it is a digital sensor that transmits its value as SENT or CAN messages. The controller sets it once those messages stop or keep failing their checks, for instance after a broken signal wire, a lost 5 V supply or a fault inside the sensor module, an electronics box that on active sensors must tolerate up to 140 °C beneath the car.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp
Exhaust temperature for bank 2 sensor 2 missing in live data
c: Sensor wiring chafed or melted along the bank 2 exhaust
5 V supply or ground to the sensor interrupted
Heat-damaged electronics module of the sensor

U0623.d: Coolant pump A is an electric pump whose speed is set over a digital link, typically LIN, and which reports its status back. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) call it the auxiliary electric water pump and fail U0623 as Type B when its response frame is absent for 2.5 s although the LIN channel is ready and either the actuator relay or the powertrain relay is energised.
s: Check engine light
Reduced cabin heat or failed scheduled preconditioning on plug-in hybrids
Other LIN device codes (grille shutters, fans) stored at the same time
c: Chafed or pinched LIN harness shared with other actuators (GM 23-NA-102)
Outdated hybrid or inverter controller software (Stellantis 08-399-25)
Blown fuse, relay or open supply/ground to the pump

U0624.d: Some engines carry a second electric coolant pump, for instance one that keeps coolant moving through the turbocharger after shutdown or feeds a separate heater or low-temperature loop. Which pump is B is decided by the manufacturer.
s: Warning lamp
Reduced heater output or higher component temperatures after shutdown
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to pump B damaged
Fuse or relay feeding pump B open
Pump electronics failed, sometimes after overheating or a seized rotor

U0625.d: Direct-injection engines increasingly use rail pressure sensors that send pressure, and sometimes fuel temperature, digitally via SENT. U0625 says the engine controller has lost this link for the bank 1 sensor.
s: Check engine light in the first trip
Reduced power, rough running or hard starting
Further SENT codes such as U101B stored at the same time
c: SENT signal wire shorted to ground or to voltage, or open
Fuel or oil contamination, corrosion or loose pins in the sensor connector
Rail pressure sensor electronics failed (on some engines only with the rail)
SENT input of the engine controller faulty

U0626.d: Without a refrigerant pressure reading the climate controller cannot protect the compressor or schedule the condenser fan. When pressure sensor A digitizes its value itself and transmits it as a LIN or SENT frame, U0626 marks that the frame has stopped arriving; which point of the circuit gets the letter A is up to the manufacturer.
s: A/C compressor stays off, no cooling
A/C fault message or flashing A/C indicator
Other LIN devices on the same line may also report no communication
c: LIN wire to the sensor pinched, chafed or cut (Audi documents this for G395)
Corroded, loose or pushed-back terminals at the sensor connector
Sensor supply voltage missing or ground intermittently open
Sensor electronics failed, often after moisture or refrigerant leaking at the sensor

U0627.d: Refrigerant temperature matters most where a controller adjusts superheat itself, as with electronic expansion valves and heat pumps; it also guards against overheated discharge gas. U0627 is set once the digital temperature value from sensor A is no longer received.
s: Reduced cooling or heat-pump output
Heat-pump mode unavailable, auxiliary heater takes over
A/C fault message
c: Connector, LIN line or supply of a combined pressure/temperature sensor faulty
Temperature channel or sensor electronics failed
Climate or thermal controller no longer polls the sensor (software or LIN master fault)

U0628.d: A second pressure transducer appears mainly in heat pumps and CO2 (R744) systems, where both the low and the high side are measured to control efficiency and detect leaks; the Sensata R744 presentation lists heat-pump control and leak diagnosis among those uses. U0628 means that the digital pressure value from sensor B no longer reaches its controller.
s: Heat pump does not heat, cabin heating relies on the auxiliary heater
Weak or no A/C cooling
A/C or thermal system warning message
c: Damaged LIN, supply or ground wire in the branch to sensor B
Wet, corroded or loose connector at sensor B

U0629.d: A second refrigerant temperature point is typical where an electronic expansion valve meters flow, for instance at the evaporator or chiller outlet, so that superheat can be calculated from temperature and pressure. U0629 is logged when the controller stops getting answers from temperature sensor B over its serial link.
s: Battery cooling or heat-pump mode unavailable
Uneven or reduced A/C performance
c: LIN line or connector at temperature sensor B open, shorted or corroded
Combined pressure/temperature unit B failed (often together with U0628)
Fuse or supply feed for sensor B open

U062A.d: Heat pumps and battery-cooling circuits need valves that redirect refrigerant, for example hot gas from the outer heat exchanger to an inner one when the system switches from cooling to heating. Suppliers such as Egelhof build these as motor-driven switching valves that replace two or more solenoid valves and are commanded digitally, partly via LIN.
s: Switching between cooling and heat-pump mode fails
No cabin heat from the heat pump or no cooling in one branch
Thermal system warning, possibly reduced charging or drive power
c: LIN, supply or ground wire to valve actuator A damaged
Moisture or corrosion in the actuator connector
Software fault in the controlling module (reprogramming may be needed)

U062B.d: Valve B is a further refrigerant switching point, for instance one that opens or closes a rear evaporator or a battery chiller path; the assignment of letters differs from maker to maker. U062B records that actuator B has stopped responding to its digital commands.
s: One cooling branch (rear A/C or battery chiller) does not work
Several heat-pump modes unavailable at once with a multi-way valve
Thermal system warning message
c: Wiring fault in the branch to valve actuator B
Loose or corroded connector at actuator B
Actuator B electronics or motor unit failed

U062C.d: A third distribution valve only exists in elaborate thermal systems that combine cabin cooling, heat pump, dehumidification and battery conditioning in one refrigerant loop. U062C is stored when valve actuator C fails to reply on its serial line.
s: A single heat-pump or dehumidifying mode no longer works
Windows fog more easily in heating mode
Climate system warning or reduced comfort without warning
c: Shared LIN segment, splice or supply feeding valve C damaged (often with U062D)
Connector at actuator C loose, wet or corroded

U062D.d: Actuator D is the fourth refrigerant switching valve and appears only in loops with many separately controlled paths; because a single multi-way unit can replace up to four solenoid valves, many vehicles never use the letter D. U062D means the controller sent requests to valve D and got no valid answer within its expected schedule.
s: One refrigerant path cannot be opened or closed
Reduced heating or cooling in certain modes
c: Supply or ground of actuator D missing (no current draw when commanded)
LIN line to actuator D open or shorted

U062E.d: An electronic expansion valve uses a geared or stepper motor to set the refrigerant flow into an evaporator or battery chiller, guided by pressure and temperature readings instead of a thermostatic bulb. Units such as Egelhof's EXV and KXV accept their target position over LIN and carry a position sensor, so they can also shut a branch completely.
s: No cooling at the affected evaporator or chiller
Cooling-system warning, possibly reduced drive or charging power on electrified vehicles
Heat pump unavailable
c: LIN, supply or ground wire to the expansion valve damaged
Connector at the valve wet or corroded (often near the evaporator or chiller)
Software fault in the thermal or powertrain controller

U062F.d: GM assigns coolant pump C to the pump of its low-temperature coolant loop, a separate circuit that runs well below engine temperature. The 2020 table 20OBDG04 fails U062F once LIN communication errors reach three counts, provided the bus itself is not already faulted (U1345), the pump is configured as present and run/crank voltage is at least 11 V.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Parts on the low-temperature loop may run hotter than normal
c: LIN wire, supply or ground to the low-temperature loop pump damaged
LIN master in the engine controller faulty

U0630.d: Engines with split or multi-zone cooling may measure coolant temperature at more than three points, and a sensor that sends its value as a digital message instead of a resistance can be checked for silence. U0630 means the engine controller no longer receives such messages from coolant temperature sensor 4.
s: Check engine light
Cooling fan may run more than usual
c: Data, supply or ground wire to sensor 4 open or shorted

U0631.d: Sensor 5 is the highest-numbered engine coolant temperature input in the J2012 list and is found only on engines that monitor many coolant zones, for example block, head, radiator outlet and separate loops. U0631 records that the controller has stopped receiving digital messages from that sensor.
s: Check engine light
Fan running more often or longer
c: Wiring to sensor 5 damaged (open, short, chafing)
Connector at sensor 5 corroded or not latched
Sensor 5 electronics failed or sending corrupt frames
Shared supply or data line fault (often with U0630)

U0632.d: Many radiator fans now contain their own speed controller and take commands over LIN instead of relays. U0632 is set when fan 1 stops responding.
s: Fan running continuously at full speed, loud
Check engine light and coolant warning message
On some Audi models limited engine speed or drive system fault message
c: Fan harness chafed or pinched near the radiator or plenum (Audi bulletins)
Fan power feed (fusible link) or ground open
Outdated software in the controller that runs the LIN bus (Mercedes PTCU)
Electronics in fan 1 failed (replaced as fan assembly)

U0633.d: U0633 is the counterpart for a second LIN-controlled radiator fan. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B checks the frame CFM2_RSP and fails after 2.5 s of silence as Type B; 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 count three missing frames, and on those engines fans 3 and 4 have their own codes on another LIN line.
s: Remaining fan runs at full speed or noise from the fan area
Warning lamp; on Audi models limited performance and engine speed
Rising coolant temperature in slow traffic
c: Fan 2 harness rubbing on the frame rail or radiator support
Power feed or ground of fan 2 interrupted

U0634.d: Liquid-cooled traction batteries check how warm the coolant is where it enters or leaves the pack to decide whether to cool or heat. Where that sensor is a digital node rather than a plain thermistor, the battery or thermal controller can detect when its messages stop, and U0634 records exactly that for sensor A.
s: Hybrid or battery warning lamp, on hybrids also the MIL
Reduced charging power or limited electric performance
c: Data, supply or ground wire to sensor A damaged
Connector at the battery coolant line corroded or loose
Battery or thermal management controller fault

U0635.d: Sensor B is the second battery coolant temperature point, commonly placed on the opposite side of the pack from sensor A so the controller can see how much heat the coolant picks up. U0635 means sensor B no longer delivers digital messages.
s: Battery or hybrid system warning
Battery cooling runs more often or charging power is reduced
c: Wiring branch to sensor B open, shorted or chafed
Moisture or corrosion at the sensor B connector

U0636.d: Battery thermal loops use motor-driven valves to send coolant through the chiller, the heater or a bypass, or to link the battery loop with the drive unit circuit. Many of these valves have a small controller of their own: Hutchinson's rotary three-way valve for electric vehicles talks LIN, and Thomas offers its coolant valves with PWM, LIN or CAN control and an optional self-diagnosis.
s: Battery or hybrid system warning
Reduced fast-charging power or limited drive power when the battery is hot or cold
Cabin heating or cooling behaving differently
c: LIN, supply or ground wire to valve A damaged
Thermal or battery controller software fault

U0637.d: Valve B is a second smart valve in the battery coolant loop, for example a mixing valve that blends chilled and warm coolant or a switch-over valve to the drive unit circuit. U0637 is set when valve B goes silent on its data link while the controller may still talk to valve A.
s: Battery or hybrid system warning
Limited charging or drive power in hot or cold weather
c: Wiring branch to valve B open, shorted or chafed
Valve B connector loose or corroded
Valve B actuator failed, sometimes after a jammed valve body

U0638.d: The coolant loop that serves the inverter and other high-voltage electronics needs its own temperature reading so the controller can size pump speed and decide when to derate. When sensor A on that loop is a bus node that sends its value digitally, for instance over LIN, the receiving controller notices when frames stop coming, and U0638 records that silence.
s: Hybrid system warning, on hybrids usually the MIL as well
Reduced electric drive power, especially under load or in hot weather
Electronics coolant pump running continuously at high speed
c: Data, supply or ground line to sensor A open, shorted or chafed
Corroded or loose connector at the electronics coolant line
Internal electronics of sensor A failed
Fault or outdated software in the controller that polls the sensor

U0639.d: A second temperature point in the electronics cooling loop, labelled B, lets the controller compare inlet and outlet or watch a separate branch, and the pair is checked against each other by P2D2A. U0639 means that sensor B, read as a digital bus participant, has gone quiet while the bus itself is still working.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning lamp
Correlation checks between the electronics coolant sensors disabled
Occasional power limitation on long climbs or fast charging
c: Harness to sensor B damaged, for example near hoses or brackets
Moisture or bent pins in the sensor B connector
Sensor B itself no longer transmits

U063A.d: Sensor C is the third digitally connected temperature sensor in the cooling loop for the hybrid or EV power electronics. It is found where a system splits the loop further, for example to give a DC/DC converter or onboard charger its own reading.
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp
Possible reduction of charging or drive power
c: Open or chafed wire in the branch that feeds sensor C only
Sensor C connector unplugged after service work or corroded

U063B.d: Rotary coolant valves are often moved by a smart actuator that takes its target angle over LIN and reports back. U063B covers the case where actuator A no longer replies.
s: Check engine light with coolant service message
Radiator fan permanently running at full speed and noisy
Further LIN codes (fan, coolant pumps, exhaust flap) stored together
c: Outdated drivetrain controller software (Mercedes PTCU version 22A)
Damaged, chafed or corroded LIN wiring or intermediate connectors
Electronics in valve actuator A failed
Missing supply voltage or ground at the actuator

U063C.d: U063C is the counterpart for the second networked coolant bypass actuator, B. Stellantis lists it for the 3.0-litre Hurricane straight six: bulletin 18-071-26 (2025 Ram 1500) and bulletins 18-082-26 and 18-083-26 (2025 Jeep Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer) name U063C next to the circuit and performance codes P0E7C to P0E7F of the same valve.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Codes P0E7C to P0E7F for bypass valve B stored at the same time
Irregular warm-up or weak cabin heat
c: Bus, supply or ground wire to actuator B damaged
Loose or corroded actuator B connector

U063D.d: The first electric pump of the power electronics loop, A, circulates coolant through the inverter, DC/DC converter and similar parts. Pumps of this class, such as Bosch's PAD2, take their speed command via PWM or LIN and run their own diagnosis; with LIN the controller also expects regular status replies.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced electric drive power or engine kept running on hybrids
Inverter or electronics overtemperature messages
c: Blown fuse or open supply/ground to electronics coolant pump A
LIN wire to the pump open, shorted or chafed
Pump electronics failed, often after running dry or overheating
Fault in the hybrid or thermal controller acting as bus master

U063E.d: Exhaust heat recovery passes hot exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start, so the engine and cabin warm up sooner; a flap later diverts the gas around it. When that flap's actuator is a LIN slave, losing it gives U063E.
s: MIL after two drive cycles
Slower engine and cabin warm-up in cold weather
Engine runs longer on hybrids to reach operating temperature
c: Actuator electronics damaged by heat near the exhaust
LIN or supply wiring under the vehicle damaged or corroded
Water ingress or corrosion in the actuator connector
Weak 12 V supply interrupting LIN communication

U063F.d: The coolant flow control valve meters how much coolant passes through the engine, and its position sensor often transmits over SENT, a one-way digital protocol with a frame every few milliseconds. U063F flags the loss of that stream.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Coolant temperature control less precise, slower warm-up or higher temperatures
c: Engine harness chafed through to the SENT, supply or ground wire (GM 21-NA-149)
Corroded or loose connector at the flow control valve
Position sensor electronics in the valve failed (usually replaced with the valve)
SENT input of the engine control module faulty

U0640.d: Many fuel tank pressure senders also measure the temperature of the vapor in the tank, and when such a sender reports digitally, typically over SENT, both values share one data stream. U0640 is stored when the engine controller no longer receives valid temperature data from this sensor.
s: Check engine light on
Often stored together with U0641
Evaporative system monitor does not complete
c: Interference or chafing on the shared signal line of the tank pressure/temperature sender
Loose or corroded connector at the tank sender
Electronics of the sender failed (only if the code is stored permanently)
Engine controller software or input fault

U0641.d: Pressure sensor A is the main input for the evaporative leak test that CARB 1968.2 (e)(4) requires: with the system sealed, the controller follows how pressure in tank and canister rises or falls. Newer designs often use a relative pressure sensor with SENT output; Melexis' MLX90821, for example, spans about −0.06 to 0.26 bar in its SENT version and can add a media temperature.
s: MIL on
EVAP leak monitor not ready, possible inspection failure
No noticeable change in driving
c: Electrical interference or damage on the sensor signal line
Connector at the tank or canister sensor loose, wet or corroded
Pressure sensor A itself no longer sends

U0642.d: A second EVAP pressure sensor, B, appears where one reading is not enough, for instance when tank and canister are separated by an isolation valve and each side needs its own value, as in sealed tanks of plug-in hybrids that see higher pressures. Which location is called B is up to the manufacturer.
s: MIL on
EVAP monitor incomplete
On sealed tanks possibly a delayed fuel door release
c: Signal, supply or ground line to sensor B open or chafed
Corroded or unplugged connector at sensor B
Receiving controller input or software fault

U0643.d: This sensor reports a temperature at charger A, whose exact measuring point the J2012 title leaves open; depending on the design it can watch the compressor outlet or the hot side. GM's tables define charger A as the first one in the exhaust path on series layouts and the bank 1 charger on parallel ones.
s: MIL on
Reduced boost and power
Further boost-related codes stored
c: Wiring near the charger damaged by heat or chafing

U0644.d: Pneumatic wastegates have largely given way to electric actuators, and these carry a position sensor so the controller knows how far the bypass flap around the turbine is open. GM reads that sensor on charger A over SENT and, in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B, stores U0644 when message faults appear or a frame is older than 3.13 ms in 10 out of 12 samples taken every 100 ms, with relay voltage of at least 11 V and the engi
s: MIL on from the first trip
Reduced engine power, boost limited
Several other engine codes when the harness is damaged
c: Engine harness chafed at brackets or covers
Connector at the wastegate actuator loose or corroded
Position sensor in the actuator failed
Low supply voltage or poor ground

U0645.d: An active air dam is a motor-driven panel below the front bumper that drops at highway speed to cut drag and retracts for low speed or rough ground. Its small control module talks to the powertrain controller over a serial line; on the 2.7L F-150 Ford runs it on a LIN bus shared with the generator and the grille shutters.
s: Air dam stays in one position
Check engine light on some trucks (Ram)
Charging system warning if the shared LIN line is shorted (Ford)
c: Air dam unit with built-in module failed (early Ram 1500 DT)
Air dam damaged by curb, snow or debris impact
Water or corrosion in the air dam connector
Shared LIN wire chafed to ground near the engine mount (Ford F-150 2.7L)

U0646.d: In these titles, motor electronics stands for the power electronics that feed an electric drive motor in a hybrid or EV, and coolant pump A is the main electric pump of that loop. When it is commanded by LIN rather than a plain PWM wire, the controlling module can tell when the pump stops talking, which is what U0646 stores.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Limited drive motor torque or power
Motor electronics over-temperature message, see P0A7C
c: Fuse, relay or power feed of motor electronics pump A interrupted
LIN line between controller and pump damaged

U0647.d: Cars fitted with two or more drive units, or with separate loops for the motor and its inverter, may fit a second networked pump in the motor electronics circuit, called B. U0647 is logged when this pump no longer returns its status frames.
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp, MIL on hybrids
Power limited on one drive unit
c: Wiring branch or fuse that serves only pump B open
Pump B connector corroded or not fully seated

U0648.d: U0648 belongs to a third digitally controlled pump in the motor electronics cooling, labelled C, which only more elaborate layouts carry, for example a generator inverter with its own loop. The fault means the pump has dropped off the bus.
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp
Reduced power from the electric machine cooled by pump C
c: Shared fuse or ground point of the pumps faulty (several pump codes at once)
Data or supply line to pump C damaged

U0649.d: Coolant pump D is the fourth auxiliary electric pump in the generic lettering that runs from A (U0623) through B and C (U0624, U062F) to E (U0698). What D circulates is up to the manufacturer; GM, for example, assigns C to its low-temperature loop, while Mercedes uses the E code for a pump of its low-temperature circuit.
s: Warning lamp, depending on manufacturer the MIL
Components on the affected loop run warmer than normal
c: LIN, supply or ground wire to pump D damaged
Controller acting as LIN master faulty or needing a software update

U064A.d: Battery management needs the pack current to count charge in and out and to judge state of charge and state of health. Many packs measure it with a self-contained sensor that sends its value over CAN; LEM's CAB series, for example, transmits on high-speed CAN at 500 kbit/s and is built for ASIL C.
s: Hybrid or EV battery warning, on hybrids also the MIL
Strongly reduced drive power or charging refused
Implausible state-of-charge display
c: CAN, supply or ground wiring of sensor A inside or at the pack damaged
Moisture or corrosion at the pack's low-voltage connector
Battery energy control module fault or software

U064B.d: Some packs carry a second current sensor, B, often a different measuring principle than A, so that the battery controller can cross-check the two through P0B13 and still have a value if one fails. U064B is stored when that second digital sensor goes silent.
s: Battery system warning lamp
Correlation check between the current sensors no longer possible
Possibly reduced charging or drive power
c: Bus or supply wiring of sensor B damaged
Missing or faulty CAN termination in the pack sub-network

U064C.d: A third pack current sensor, C, appears where a battery has parallel strings or a separate measuring point, for instance in a battery junction box, that each need their own current value. U064C means that this sensor no longer delivers its data frames to the battery controller.
s: Battery warning lamp
Reduced power and slower charging
c: Data or supply wiring of sensor C damaged
Loose connector at the battery junction box

U064D.d: Trucks with a factory trailer brake controller carry a dash switch with gain buttons and a manual slider that lets the driver apply only the trailer brakes. On current designs this switch is a small electronic unit that reports to the brake controller, which is why GM's 2024 campaign N242442100 for the 2022 Silverado and Sierra pairs a new switch with reprogramming of the cluster and the brake module.
s: Service trailer brake message in the cluster
Gain buttons and manual slider have no effect
Electric trailer brakes not applied when braking
c: Trailer brake control switch electronics failed
Switch connector behind the dash trim loose or not seated
Damaged data or supply wire to the switch
Brake or cluster software not matched to a replaced switch

U064E.d: Many diesels steer recirculated exhaust around the EGR cooler while the engine is cold and through it once warm, using a bypass flap with its own position sensor. CARB 1968.2 (f)(6.2.5) requires the cooler system to be checked for poor cooling, and that check only makes sense if the controller knows the flap position.
s: MIL on
EGR cooler monitor not completed
Usually no change in driving behaviour
c: Wiring to the cooler bypass actuator damaged by heat or vibration
Corroded or loose connector at the bypass actuator
Position sensor in the bypass actuator failed

U064F.d: Diesel swirl flaps partly close one intake port per cylinder at low load so the charge spins and mixes better; a motor moves them and a sensor reports the angle. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B that sensor transmits by SENT, and U064F covers a missing or corrupt stream: an internal fault flag or message error, or position data not refreshed for over 6.25 ms with the line held steadily high or low.
s: MIL after two trips with the fault
Swirl flaps left in default position, slightly rougher or smokier low-load running
Often no noticeable change in driving
c: Position sensor in the swirl flap actuator failed
Oil or soot in the actuator connector, corroded pins
SENT signal wire chafed, open or shorted on the engine

U0650.d: The exhaust pressure control valve is a throttle flap in the exhaust that diesels use to raise back pressure and exhaust temperature, for example during warm-up or filter regeneration. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B this flap is called ETV and reports its position by SENT.
s: MIL on from the first trip
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or blocked
Slower warm-up in cold weather
c: Wiring at the exhaust flap damaged by heat
Connector at the flap actuator corroded or loose
Position sensor in the flap actuator failed

U0651.d: EGR sensors A to D are generic slots: a maker may assign them to valve position, pressure or another EGR measurement. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B, which has both a high-pressure and a low-pressure EGR loop, sensor A is the SENT position sensor of the high-pressure valve.
s: MIL on from the first trip
EGR switched off, possibly louder combustion
EGR monitor not ready
c: SENT line to the EGR valve damaged by heat or chafing
EGR valve connector corroded or loose
Position sensor in the EGR valve failed

U0652.d: U0652 covers a digital EGR sensor labelled B that has stopped delivering data. What B measures depends on the maker; it may be the position of a second valve or a pressure or temperature signal of the EGR path.
s: MIL on
EGR monitor incomplete
Possibly reduced EGR operation
c: Wiring to EGR sensor B open, shorted or heat-damaged
Connector at sensor B corroded or loose

U0653.d: On GM's 2025 diesel with high- and low-pressure EGR (table 25OBDG04B), EGR sensor C is the SENT position sensor of the low-pressure valve, which as usual for such loops takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it ahead of the compressor. Oddly, the table's text calls this valve the B position sensor while filing its codes under C.
s: MIL on from the first trip
Low-pressure EGR disabled, higher NOx
EGR monitor not ready
c: Wiring to the low-pressure EGR valve damaged near the exhaust
Position sensor in the low-pressure EGR valve failed

U0654.d: Diesel intake air flow valve A is the throttle ahead of the intake manifold: it creates the vacuum for high EGR rates, trims airflow for filter regeneration and shuts at switch-off. GM's 2025 diesel tables 25OBDG04A and 25OBDG04B read its angle by SENT and set U0654 when the data stop refreshing for more than 6.25 ms while the line is stuck low or high, a frame is faulty, or the counters freeze.
s: MIL in the first trip
EGR control restricted, particulate filter regeneration delayed
Engine may shake more at switch-off
c: Oil, soot or corrosion in the throttle body connector
SENT signal, supply or ground wire damaged
Position sensor in the throttle unit failed (usually replaced with the unit)

U0655.d: Some diesels carry a second intake air flow valve, labelled B; which flap gets that letter depends on the engine layout and the maker. When its angle sensor is a digital SENT unit, U0655 reports that the engine controller no longer receives usable position frames from it.
s: Check engine light
Particulate filter regeneration postponed or blocked
Little change in drivability in many cases
c: Contaminated or loose connector at throttle unit B
Signal, supply or ground wire to sensor B damaged
Digital position sensor of valve B failed

U0656.d: On a variable geometry turbocharger the boost control position sensor reports where the guide vanes stand, and the controller needs that feedback to regulate boost and to check, as CARB 1968.2 (f)(7.2.3) asks, that the vanes reach their target in time. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B reads this VGT position by SENT and sets U0656 when 480 of 600 checks, run every 6.25 ms, find the protocol stuck low or high with sta
s: MIL on
Limp mode with clearly reduced power
Boost control codes stored at the same time
c: SENT, supply or ground line to the VGT actuator damaged
Connector at the actuator exposed to heat, oil or water
Position sensor or electronics in the VGT actuator failed
Engine controller input or software fault

U0657.d: The bypass valve meant here sits on the intake side: on turbocharged petrol engines it lets compressed air recirculate when the throttle shuts, and on supercharged engines it routes air around the blower at light load. When the valve is electrically driven and reports its position digitally, U0657 marks that the position data from valve A has stopped arriving.
s: MIL on
Less boost or hesitant throttle response
Unusual whoosh or flutter when lifting off
c: Wiring to the bypass valve open, shorted or chafed
Position sensor in the valve failed

U0658.d: To keep the glass clear before it mists, an automatic climate system can compare the temperature of the inner windshield surface with the cabin air's dew point right in front of it. Suppliers such as Sensirion (SAAF) and ScioSense (WSS2) build this into one small module at the mirror base that computes the dew point itself and reports over LIN at 19.2 kBd.
s: Windshield fogs before the climate system responds
Automatic defog or anti-fog function inactive or less effective
Other sensors on the same mirror-base LIN line may also be missing
c: Sensor not clipped back, unplugged or without glass contact after windshield replacement
Loose or damaged plug or LIN wire at the mirror base or headliner
Electronics of the humidity and glass temperature module failed
Code logged in a wake-up phase such as remote start without a real fault

U0659.d: In a two-zone system the left front temperature actuator turns the blend door that sets how much of the air for the left side passes the heater core. As a smart LIN node it takes position requests from the climate master and replies with its state.
s: Left zone stuck hot or cold regardless of the setting
Check engine light on GM vehicles that list the code as Type B
Climate display may show a fault or ignore left temperature changes
c: Electronics of the left temperature actuator failed
LIN, supply or ground wire to the actuator open or chafed under the dash
Actuator plug not latched after dash or footwell work
Configuration or software fault in the module that polls the actuator

U065A.d: The right front temperature actuator only exists where the right-hand front seat gets its own blend door, as in dual-zone systems; single-zone cars move one door for both sides and never run this check. GM lists U065A next to U0659 in its 2025 BCM tables, watching the frame AHDA05_Rsp with the same 11.5 s limit and Type B rating; in 25OBDG04B that slave is calibrated as not present, so the monitor stays idle on that
s: Passenger side blows hot or cold no matter what is selected
Right temperature setting has no effect while the left side works
MIL possible on GM models with the code rated Type B
c: Right temperature actuator electronics or motor failed
Wire to the actuator damaged behind the glovebox or console side panel
Climate module configured for the wrong number of zones after replacement

U065B.d: The mode actuator decides where the air leaves the dash: face vents, footwell or windshield. A separate left front unit points to a layout where each front zone has its own distribution door; when the climate master gets no reply from it over LIN, U065B is stored.
s: Left outlets keep blowing at face, floor or glass regardless of mode
Defrost selection does not move air to the left part of the windshield
Climate fault message or flashing mode indicator
c: Break or short on the LIN branch to the left mode actuator
Shared actuator supply or ground missing

U065C.d: A right front mode actuator lets the passenger side choose its own outlets, or in some designs close its share of the air altogether; Denso's US 2020/0189351 describes a passenger-side door driven by its own actuator so that only the driver is served. U065C means the climate master can no longer reach that right-hand unit over LIN.
s: Passenger outlets ignore mode changes
Little or no airflow on the passenger side
Uneven comfort between driver and passenger
c: Connector on the passenger side of the HVAC case loose or wet
Damaged LIN branch toward the passenger side

U065D.d: The air intake actuator swings the inlet door between outside air and cabin air. Modern controllers move it on their own: Ford's SSM 51726 notes that the 2021-23 Bronco opens the inlet door to about half every 30 to 60 minutes in recirculation to refresh the cabin, and onsemi's TND416 describes stepper-driven recirculation flaps that find their end stop by stall detection and save compressor energy by reusing cooled
s: Recirculation button has no effect
Windows fog quickly when the door is stuck on recirculation
Outside smells enter the cabin when it is stuck on fresh air
c: Water ingress at the blower housing reaching the actuator plug
LIN or supply wire to the inlet actuator damaged

U065E.d: At speed, the wind pushes extra outside air through the cowl inlet into the climate housing. Some vehicles therefore fit the fresh-air path with a motorised ram air flap that narrows the opening as dynamic pressure rises, so airflow and noise stay steady; Behr's US 5,645,479 nests it with the recirculation flap, and Daimler's DE 10 2010 025 623 drives it through a non-linear linkage for fine throttling near closed.
s: Airflow rises noticeably with road speed
Air rush noise from the vents at high speed
Weak airflow at low speed if the flap stopped nearly closed
c: Ram air flap actuator electronics failed
Moisture or debris from the cowl reaching the actuator connector
LIN wire to the ram air actuator chafed or disconnected

U065F.d: Vehicles with a separately controlled rear climate zone need their own temperature doors for the rear outlets, and in a split rear system the left side may use two of them, labelled A and B. Hanon's US 11,305,608 shows why two can be needed: one door ahead of the heater core and a second behind it mixing warm air into the rear cold-air duct.
s: Often none when the code is only stored as history
Rear left air stays hot or cold
Rear temperature control has no effect on the left
c: Software timing between modules logs a false history code (GM)
Left rear temperature actuator A failed
Rear HVAC harness or connector damaged in the floor or rear quarter

U0660.d: Temperature actuator B is the second door for the same rear left zone that A serves. Where a rear zone uses two doors, one typically sets the split between cold and heated air and the other trims the mix further downstream, like the downstream rear door in Hanon's US 11,305,608; makers do not publish which letter goes to which.
s: Rear left temperature drifts or overshoots the set value
Rear left zone reacts slowly to temperature changes
c: Actuator B electronics or motor failed
Fault in the wiring branch or plug that only actuator B uses
Replacement actuator not assigned or calibrated by the scan tool

U0661.d: A right rear temperature actuator is only fitted where the rear seats are split into left and right climate zones, as in four-zone systems of large sedans, SUVs and vans. Actuator A on the right is the counterpart of U065F on the left, so when this code is stored the passenger behind the front passenger seat loses temperature control while the left rear zone still works.
s: Right rear zone stays at one temperature
Rear right temperature buttons have no effect
Left rear zone continues to work normally
c: Right rear temperature actuator A failed
Actuator plug in the right rear duct area loose or corroded
Shared rear LIN segment faulty (then usually several rear codes)

U0662.d: With four rear temperature actuators, A and B on each side, plus front units, a climate system may run many look-alike motors on LIN, where one master serves up to 15 slaves. Identical parts must be told apart, either by part variant or by position detection along a daisy chain, as the LIN article explains.
s: Right rear temperature imprecise or slow to settle
Code appears right after an actuator was replaced
c: Replacement or swapped actuator B without the correct LIN address
Open supply, ground or LIN pin at actuator B

U0663.d: The rear mode actuator steers rear-seat air between upper outlets, such as console or roof vents, and the rear footwell. Hanon's US 11,305,608 shows a dome-shaped rear mode door doing exactly this between console vent and rear floor vent.
s: No symptom if the code is only stored as history
Rear air stuck at the console or roof vents or at the floor
Rear mode button has no effect
c: Software timing in the body or climate module storing a false history code (GM)
Harness to the rear HVAC unit or console damaged

U0664.d: Some climate units carry a door that opens or shuts the whole air supply to the rear seats, so the system can send everything forward when nobody sits in the back or when the front needs full airflow. Hanon's US 11,305,608 places such an on-off door on the rear cold-air passage, and Denso's US 2020/0189351 moves its rear airflow door to feed or close the rear vent and heat outlets.
s: No air at the rear outlets
Rear outlets keep blowing although rear climate is off
Reduced airflow at the front during maximum cooling or defrost
c: Actuator plug at the rear outlet of the HVAC case not seated
LIN or supply wire to the cutoff actuator damaged

U0665.d: Engines with one fuel rail per cylinder bank may give each rail its own pressure sensor, and newer ones send the reading digitally via SENT. U0665 says the controller has lost the bank 2 sensor's data.
s: Check engine light after one trip
Reduced power, hesitation or rough running
GM-specific code U101C stored alongside
c: Bank 2 sensor signal wire open or shorted to ground or voltage
Fuel-soaked, corroded or loose sensor connector
Rail pressure sensor electronics on bank 2 failed

U0666.d: The reductant pressure sensor watches the DEF line between the supply pump and the dosing valve. Bosch, for instance, offers its supply module with or without such a sensor; with it, the pump only runs when dosing is requested, the line stays pressurised through stop-start phases and is purged at key-off against freezing.
s: DEF system warning in the cluster
Dosing stopped, higher NOx output
Check engine light possible
c: DEF crystals or corrosion in the supply module connector
Harness to the tank or pump module damaged
Pressure sensor failed (often only with the pump module)
Fault in the dosing or engine control unit input

U0667.d: Engine oil temperature feeds warm-up strategies, injection and protection functions, and on recent engines the sensor sends it digitally over SENT. U0667 says that link has failed.
s: Check engine light
P0195 stored at the same time
Oil temperature reading missing in the cluster or scan tool
c: Oil wicking into the sensor connector
Sensor signal, 5 V supply or ground wire damaged

U0668.d: Despite the word circuit in its name, U0668 concerns the data link to the oil level sensor, not a voltage fault. Sensors in the sump measure the oil height either thermally or by ultrasound; Hella's PULS type packs an ultrasonic transducer, a temperature sensor and an ASIC into one module that sends its result to the engine controller over a single signal line, and loss of supply or ground is one listed failure cause
s: Oil level warning or service message in the display
Oil level reading unavailable
c: Missing supply voltage or ground at the sensor
Sensor electronics failed or oil inside the housing
Corroded or damaged connector or harness at the oil pan

U0669.d: Two makers document sensor D as an EGR pressure sensor with SENT output. Ford's 2024–2025 gasoline OBD summary lists U0669 as EGR sensor D communication for the SENT EGR pressure sensor it calls DPFE (range 0.1 to 408.8 kPa): it is checked continuously while the EGR monitor runs and flags a fault when the sensor stops talking or sends corrupt data, after about 5 seconds.
s: MIL on
EGR flow monitor does not run
Sometimes rough idle or pinging when EGR is shut off
c: SENT, supply or ground line to the EGR pressure sensor damaged
Connector at the pressure sensor corroded or loose
Engine controller input or software fault

U066A.d: EGR sensors A to E are open slots in the code set: each maker decides whether a slot carries a valve position, a pressure or a differential pressure in the recirculation path. U066A means the engine controller no longer gets usable digital frames from the device it calls sensor E, typically a SENT part.
s: Check engine light
EGR switched off or limited, sometimes harsher combustion noise
EGR readiness monitor not complete
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to EGR sensor E damaged by heat or chafing
Connector at the sensor loose, corroded or contaminated with soot
Engine controller input or software fault

U066B.d: When the throttle snaps shut, a compressor bypass valve lets boosted air recirculate to the inlet side instead of surging against the closed plate. Engines with two chargers or two compressor stages can carry a second such valve, and if its electric actuator reports the opening angle as a digital message, U066B means the engine controller no longer gets valid position frames from valve B.
s: Check engine light
Boost limited, reduced power
Compressor surge noise when lifting off the throttle
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to the bypass valve B actuator damaged
Connector at the valve loose, corroded or heat-damaged near the turbo
Position sensor electronics in the valve actuator failed
Engine controller input or software fault

U066C.d: Exhaust heat recovery sends hot gas through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start and later steers it past; the steering is done by bypass flaps. Actuator B is the second such flap, present only where the layout has two paths or stages.
s: Check engine light, on some systems only after two drive cycles
Engine and cabin heater warm up more slowly
Hybrid engine runs longer to reach temperature
c: Actuator B electronics damaged by exhaust heat
LIN, supply or ground wire under the vehicle damaged
Water or salt corrosion in the actuator connector
Low supply voltage during the check

U066D.d: The temperature of the charge air behind the intercooler tells the engine controller how dense the intake charge is and whether the cooler still removes enough heat; CARB lists charge air cooler temperature in the data diesel vehicles must report and requires an undercooling monitor in (f)(7.2.4). U066D is reserved for a bank 1 sensor that delivers its reading as a digital frame, for example as the NTC channel of a S
s: Check engine light
Slightly reduced power at high load
Often no noticeable change in normal driving
c: Signal or supply wire to the charge air sensor open or chafed
Oily or corroded connector at the charge air pipe
Digital sensor (often combined with boost pressure) failed
Engine controller input or software fault

U066E.d: A bank 2 charge air temperature only exists on V or boxer engines that run one turbocharger and one intercooler per cylinder bank. There the controller can compare both sides, and a mismatch belongs to P007F, the bank 1/bank 2 correlation code.
s: Check engine light
Possible additional bank correlation code (P007F)
Mostly unchanged driving behaviour
c: Wiring to the bank 2 charge air sensor damaged, often routed near the hot side
Connector at the bank 2 charge air pipe loose or oily

U066F.d: The low-pressure side of a direct-injection fuel system runs from the tank pump to the high-pressure pump, and a sensor there lets the controller regulate the lift pump. If that sensor transmits a digital value, for example over SENT, U066F records that its messages have stopped.
s: Check engine light
Longer cranking or hard starting
Hesitation or power loss under heavy load
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to the low-pressure sensor damaged
Connector at the sensor or fuel line corroded or not latched
Sensor electronics failed and no longer transmit
Receiving input or software of the engine or pump control module faulty

U0670.d: GM's 2025 direct-injection engines measure fuel temperature in the high-pressure rail with digital SENT sensors, and sensor 1 is the one GM files under U0670. The test counts pulses on the signal wire: if the line sits permanently high and four or fewer pulses arrive (25OBDG03A; 40 or fewer in 25OBDG03B), a sample fails, and 400 bad samples in a window of 500, one every 6.25 ms, set the code; being Type A, it lights
s: Check engine light from the first trip
Usually no noticeable change in driving
Occasionally rougher hot restarts
c: SENT signal wire to sensor A shorted or open
Connector at the fuel rail loose or contaminated
Fuel temperature sensor A internally failed
SENT receiver in the engine controller faulty

U0671.d: Sensor B is the second SENT temperature sensor in GM's high-pressure fuel rail (sensor 2 in 25OBDG03A and 25OBDG03B). Its link test mirrors that of sensor A, line stuck high with too few pulses, 400 of 500 samples at 6.25 ms, Type A.
s: Check engine light
Sensor comparison and range checks of sensor B not completed
Often no drivability complaint
c: Signal wire of sensor B chafed, shorted or open
Shared 5 V supply or ground of both rail sensors faulty
Engine controller input or software fault

U0672.d: GM's 2.0 L LSY and 2.7 L L3B four-cylinders circulate coolant with an electric main pump that the engine controller commands over LIN. U0672 sets when the pump's response frame MWP_Rsp is missing for at least 250 ms (25OBDG03B; same logic in 19OBDG03D for the L3B) once the LIN channel is up, the relay is powered and battery voltage exceeds 11 V; as a Type A fault it turns the MIL on at once.
s: Check engine light immediately
Rising coolant temperature or overheating warning
Weak cabin heating
Reduced engine power to protect the engine
c: Poor terminal tension, crimp or lock at the electric pump connector
LIN, supply or ground wire to the pump chafed or contaminated
Pump relay or fuse supplying the pump faulty

U0673.d: After each spark, a small bias voltage across the plug gap lets the ignition system measure the current carried by ions in the burning mixture; Ford's patent US20170030322A1 shows such an ion sensing module passing this signal to the controller for combustion and knock assessment. U0673 means the engine controller no longer hears from that module.
s: Check engine light
Other stored codes from the same software issue
Usually no change in how the engine runs
c: Bus, supply or ground wiring of the ion sense module faulty

U0674.d: Electric wastegate actuators need position feedback so the controller can hold the turbine bypass at the commanded opening. On twin-turbo engines the second charger gets its own sensor, and U0674 says the digital frames from that sensor B have stopped or are corrupt.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power, boost limited on one charger
Sluggish response under load
c: Wiring to the wastegate B actuator heat-damaged or chafed
Position sensor inside the actuator failed
Weak supply voltage or poor ground

U0675.d: A speed sensor in the bearing or compressor housing lets the controller watch how fast the turbocharger rotor spins, mainly to keep it below its overspeed limit; a BorgWarner patent (US9353760B2) describes such a sensor and gives that reason, and CARB names turbocharger/turbine speed among the data diesel vehicles must output. Classic sensors send a pulse train whose faults are P2578 to P2582.
s: Check engine light
Boost and power limited
Noticeably weaker acceleration at higher loads
c: Sensor wiring near the turbocharger heat-damaged or broken
Engine controller input or software fault

U0676.d: Fuel level sensor A is the main tank sender. Usually it is a float-driven resistor read as a voltage, and U0676 only applies where the sender itself reports digitally and its messages stop.
s: Fuel gauge reads empty, full or freezes
Range display missing or wrong
Check engine light, EVAP readiness not set
c: Wiring at the tank or fuel pump flange damaged or corroded
Electronics of the level sender failed
Module that reads or forwards the level faulty
Connector under the vehicle not latched or water-damaged

U0677.d: A second level sender is needed when a tank has two chambers, as in saddle tanks that straddle the driveshaft, or when a vehicle carries a second tank. GM's 25OBDG03B calls it sensor 2 of the secondary tank, used on vehicles with two senders and a mechanical transfer pump; its circuit checks fail below 10 % or above 60 % of the 5 V range in 40 of 50 samples (P2067/P2068, Type B).
s: Gauge drops suddenly or never shows full
Range estimate inaccurate
Check engine light
c: Wiring to the secondary-chamber sender damaged
Connector at the secondary flange corroded

U0678.d: A third level sender only makes sense where the fuel volume is split further, for example a tank with three chambers or a main tank plus an auxiliary one. U0678 would be stored when such a sender C reports its value as a message and that message is lost.
s: Gauge or range wrong when the third chamber is involved
Check engine light
EVAP readiness not completed
c: Wiring to sender C damaged or corroded
Module receiving the level data faulty

U0679.d: Automatic transmissions measure hydraulic pressure to confirm that a clutch or pulley really received the pressure the controller asked for. Which sensor is A varies: Ford's 2024 summary calls the sensors of its 10R60/10R80 and 8F units TFP A and B, analog with 0.5 to 4.5 V for 0 to 2,500 kPa, and sets P0841 when the reading sticks although the clutch still applies and releases.
s: Harsh or delayed shifts
Transmission stays in a fixed gear
Check engine or transmission warning light
c: Transmission internal harness or lead frame to sensor A damaged
Transmission case connector leaking oil or corroded
Transmission control module input or software fault

U067A.d: Sensor B is the second pressure measuring point. In GM's CVT table 25OBDG03A it reads the secondary pulley, whose pressure sets the clamping force on the belt; its plausibility check runs only above 1,200 rpm with line pressure over 1,000 kPa and a secondary command above 500 kPa.
s: Firm shifts or engagement
Reduced engine torque, limp mode
Warning light on
c: Internal wiring to sensor B damaged
Separate sensor supply for B faulty

U067B.d: Parallel hybrids put a clutch between engine and electric motor so the car can drive electrically with the engine stopped. Many close it hydraulically, and a pressure sensor confirms the clamping: in Ford's 10R80 MHT hybrid transmission, as Gears Magazine explains, the auxiliary pump closes the clutch and a pressure sensor watches that supply.
s: Hybrid system warning, electric driving unavailable
Engine runs continuously or starts roughly
Check engine light
c: Wiring or connector of the clutch pressure sensor damaged
Transmission or hybrid controller input or software fault

U067C.d: Some engines need a third electric cooling fan, for instance for a charge-air or auxiliary radiator, and LIN lets each fan carry its own speed electronics. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B uses U067C for cooling fan 3: the response frame CFM3_Rsp must be missing for at least 2,437.5 ms, the LIN channel enabled and battery voltage above 11 V; the code is Type B, so the MIL lights after two trips.
s: Check engine light after two trips
High coolant or charge-air temperature at low speed or when towing
Fan 3 silent or running constantly
c: LIN wire to fan 3 chafed or open
High-current supply, fuse or ground of fan 3 faulty
Fan connector corroded by road spray

U067D.d: U067D is meant for a fourth cooling fan with its own network interface that has stopped answering. Four electrically commanded fans are rare.
s: Temperature climbs in traffic or under heavy load
Warning light depending on manufacturer
Fan 4 does not run
c: Fan 4 power feed or ground interrupted

U067E.d: An exhaust pressure control valve is a flap in the exhaust that diesels close partly to raise back pressure, which speeds warm-up and helps reach filter regeneration temperatures. Valve B is a second flap of this kind, and U067E concerns its position sensor or switch when that reports digitally: the controller has lost its messages.
s: Check engine light
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or not started
Longer warm-up in cold weather
c: Sensor wiring at valve B damaged by exhaust heat
Connector at valve B corroded or loose
Position sensor in the valve B unit failed
Engine controller input or software fault

U067F.d: Barometric pressure sensor A is normally the ambient sensor that corrects fueling, boost targets and many diagnostics for altitude; CARB requires barometric pressure, measured or estimated, in the OBD data stream. U067F covers a digital version of that sensor whose messages stop arriving.
s: Check engine light
Slightly off fueling or boost at altitude
Other diagnostics may be suspended
c: Data, supply or ground wire to the barometric sensor interrupted

U0680.d: The letter B need not mean a second ambient sensor; it can be any further pressure input that sees near-atmospheric air. GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 tables, written for a program with two throttle bodies, use barometric sensor B for the pressure ahead of the bank 2 throttle and send it over SENT.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Uneven running between banks possible
Additional pressure plausibility codes
c: SENT signal, supply or ground wire to the bank 2 pressure sensor faulty
Connector at the sensor ahead of the throttle loose or wet
Engine controller software or SENT input fault

U0681.d: In the generic code scheme the letters D, E and F normally mark the accelerator pedal tracks, while A to C and G belong to throttle bodies. U0681 is meant for a pedal module whose first track D reports digitally, for example over SENT or SPC as offered by Melexis' MLX90377 position IC, which lists pedal sensors as an application and comes as a fully redundant dual die.
s: Check engine light and possibly a powertrain warning
Sluggish, rate-limited throttle response
Reduced power
c: Wiring to the pedal module chafed in the footwell or at the bulkhead
Pedal module connector loose or corroded
Sensor electronics in the pedal module failed (replaced as a unit)
Engine controller input or software fault

U0682.d: Track E is usually the redundant second signal of the accelerator pedal, which the controller compares with track D before trusting any torque request. U0682 marks the loss of digital frames from that track.
s: Check engine light and powertrain warning
Delayed throttle response
Fixed elevated idle with no pedal response if both tracks fail
c: Signal or reference wire of track E damaged
Water or corrosion in the pedal connector

U0683.d: A third pedal track F is rare. It appears where a pedal module carries three signals, or where the F letter is used for an extra switch or a throttle input; the correlation codes P2139 (D/F), P2140 (E/F) and P212F (F/G) show that the scheme pairs F both with the pedal tracks and with throttle sensor G.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or limited throttle response
Additional correlation codes possible
c: Wiring for input F open, shorted or chafed
Connector at the pedal or sensor module loose or corroded
Sensor electronics for input F failed

U0684.d: A catalyst temperature sensor tells the controller when the converter is hot enough to work and to be tested. Sensor 1 on bank 1 is the first such probe on the bank that holds cylinder 1.
s: Check engine light
Catalyst readiness monitor does not complete
c: Sensor lead near the converter burnt or chafed
Evaluation electronics of the temperature sensor failed
Engine controller input or software fault

U0685.d: Where a converter carries two temperature probes, one usually sits ahead of the brick and one behind it, so that the heat released by the reaction shows up as a rise between them. Sensor 2 on bank 1 is the second, downstream position.
s: Check engine light
Catalyst monitor or sensor comparison stays incomplete
c: Lead of the downstream probe damaged by heat, stones or road salt
Connector corroded or not fully latched

U0686.d: Bank 2 exists only on engines whose cylinder rows feed separate exhaust paths, so U0686 belongs to V or flat engines with one converter per side. It means the first catalyst temperature probe of that second bank has stopped delivering digital messages.
s: Check engine light
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completed
c: Sensor electronics on bank 2 damaged by heat
Harness on the bank 2 side chafed or melted

U0687.d: U0687 refers to the rear catalyst temperature probe of bank 2, the one behind the converter brick on the second cylinder row. Once its digital messages stop, the controller can no longer compare bank 2 inlet and outlet temperatures (P046B) and loses an over-temperature guard: such probes have long been used to warn when a converter runs hotter than it can tolerate, which on older two-way designs was around 750 °C.
s: Check engine light
